I remembered what things were like during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. A carpenter in the North earned three dollars a day, measured in gold; one in the South earned fifty—paid in Confederate paper money worth a dollar a bushel. In the North a set of overalls cost three dollars, one day's pay; in the South it cost seventy-five, or two days' pay. Everything else was priced in proportion. So wages in the North were twice as high as wages in the South, because they bought twice as much.

Yes, I got to know various people in the little village, and I was particularly pleased to discover our new coins circulating there—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, quite a few nickels, and some silver, all passing among the craftsmen and ordinary people. There was even some gold, though that was at the bank, which is to say, the goldsmith's. I stepped in while Marco, son of Marco, was bargaining with a shopkeeper over a quarter pound of salt, and asked them to change a twenty-dollar gold coin. They obliged—after biting it, ringing it on the counter, testing it with acid, and asking where I had got it, who I was, where I came from, where I was heading, when I expected to arrive, and perhaps two hundred other questions. When they finally ran out, I carried on, volunteering a great deal of information: I owned a dog called Watch; my first wife had been a Free Will Baptist; her grandfather had supported Prohibition; I had once known a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip, who had died looking forward to a glorious resurrection; and so on, and on, and on. Eventually even that insatiably curious villager began to look satisfied, and a little annoyed as well. But he was bound to respect a man of my financial standing, so he kept any rude remarks to himself. I noticed, though, that he took his irritation out on his assistants, which was perfectly natural. Yes, they changed my twenty, but I thought it put a little pressure on the bank's resources. That was only to be expected: it was like stepping into some tiny nineteenth-century village shop and suddenly asking the proprietor to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. Perhaps he could manage it; but meanwhile he would be wondering how a small farmer came to have so much money in his pocket. The goldsmith was probably thinking the same thing, for he followed me to the door and stood there watching me go with respectful admiration.

Now, however, she wished it had not happened. She suspected he had enjoyed too much of Mr. Weston's excellent wine, and was certain he would want to talk nonsense.

Hoping her own manner would keep him as restrained as possible, she prepared at once to discuss the weather and the night with perfect calm and seriousness. But she had barely begun, they had barely passed through the driveway gate and drawn alongside the other carriage, when he interrupted her subject—seized her hand—insisted on her attention, and actually began declaring his love with tremendous fervour. Mr. Elton was taking full advantage of this precious opportunity, expressing feelings that surely she already knew: hoping, fearing, adoring, ready to die if she rejected him; yet confident that his burning devotion, his incomparable love, his unprecedented passion must have some effect. In short, he was thoroughly determined that she should seriously accept him as soon as possible. It was really happening. Without hesitation, without apology, without much apparent nervousness, Mr. Elton, Harriet's admirer, was announcing that he loved her. She attempted to interrupt, but in vain; he would continue until he had said everything. Angry though she was, reflection on the circumstances made her resolve to control herself when her turn to speak came. She believed drink must account for half this foolishness, and could therefore hope it would last no longer than the present hour. So she answered with a blend of seriousness and playfulness that she hoped would best suit his partly intoxicated state.

“I am very surprised, Mr. Elton. Saying this to me! You are forgetting yourself—you have mistaken me for my friend. I will gladly deliver any message for Miss Smith; but please say no more of this to me.”

“Miss Smith! A message for Miss Smith! What could she possibly mean?” He repeated her words with such a confident tone, such an arrogant display of astonishment, that she could not help answering sharply.

“Mr. Elton, this behaviour is extraordinary! I can explain it in only one way: you are not yourself, or you could never speak like this either to me or about Harriet. Control yourself enough to say nothing more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to raise his spirits, without in the least clouding his judgment. He knew exactly what he meant. After protesting vehemently that her suspicion was deeply insulting, and briefly mentioning his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—while admitting his astonishment that Miss Smith had been mentioned at all—he returned to his own passion and pressed her urgently for a favourable reply.

Lord Canterville's refusal troubled Mr. Otis considerably, and he entreated him to think the matter over again; but the kindly peer remained perfectly firm, and at last persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift bestowed upon her by the ghost. When, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire attended the Queen's first drawing-room upon her marriage, her jewels won admiration from all. For Virginia gained the coronet that rewards every good little American girl, and married her youthful lover the moment he attained his majority. They were both so delightful, and so devoted to each other, that everybody welcomed the marriage, save the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters, and had entertained at no fewer than three costly dinner-parties with that object; and, curiously enough, Mr. Otis himself. Personally, Mr. Otis liked the young Duke exceedingly, but in principle he disapproved of titles, and, in his own phrase, ‘felt some apprehension that, surrounded by the weakening influences of a pleasure-seeking aristocracy, the sound principles of republican simplicity might be forgotten.’ His objections were, however, entirely set aside, and I fancy that when he proceeded up the aisle of St. George's, Hanover Square, his daughter's hand resting on his arm, no man throughout England was prouder.

When their honeymoon had ended, the Duke and Duchess travelled down to Canterville Chase. On the afternoon following their arrival, they went on foot to the secluded churchyard beside the pine-woods. The inscription for Sir Simon's gravestone had at first occasioned considerable difficulty, but in the end it was agreed to carve only the initials of the old gentleman's name and the verse upon the library window. The Duchess had brought some beautiful roses, and scattered them over the grave. After lingering beside it a while, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the ancient abbey. Here the Duchess seated herself on a fallen column, and her husband stretched himself at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing into her lovely eyes. All at once he tossed the cigarette aside, caught her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife ought to keep no secrets from her husband.’

‘My dear Cecil! I keep none from you.’

‘Indeed you do,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never related what befell you when you were shut up with the ghost.’

‘I have told nobody, Cecil,’ Virginia answered solemnly.
